passage: Nirmala, come sit. Your mother says the stream form is due Friday and you can't sleep. Let me tell you about your uncle Gurpreet at sixteen. I had no idea what I wanted, and the deadline made my stomach flip every night. So I tried small experiments. One Saturday I sat in a print shop watching how jobs were quoted. Another day I asked our neighbour, a surveyor, what his week really looked like, the dull parts too. I picked commerce with a shrug, not certainty. At eighteen I moved to design, and nothing fell apart. The first choice was only a first choice. This weekend, go and ask someone with a real job what they do all day.

qa.q: What did Gurpreet do one Saturday as an experiment?
qa.a: Gurpreet sat in a print shop watching how jobs were quoted.

qa.q: What was Gurpreet feeling at sixteen, and what showed it?
qa.a: Gurpreet felt panicky and lost; the stomach flipping every night at the deadline and having no idea what to want show it.

qa.q: What small experiment could Nirmala try this weekend?
qa.a: Ask someone with a real job what they do all day, dull parts included, as Gurpreet asked the surveyor.

qa.q: How might Nirmala feel on hearing that a first choice can change?
qa.a: Probably relieved and less pressured, since "the first choice was only a first choice" and Gurpreet moved to design at eighteen without things falling apart.

grounding: Gurpreet recalls fear at not knowing what to choose before a deadline, and small experiments, talking to real workers and revising later.

passage: Sumit had watched three videos about architecture, all glossy buildings and sunsets, and none had made him trust anything. So during the Diwali visit he cornered Urmila didi on the balcony. "Is it really as cool as it looks?" Urmila laughed. "Honestly? The studies are long, clients change their minds at the last minute, and I've missed family dinners. But when a house I drew has people living in it, that's a good feeling." Sumit felt something settle. The bad parts made the good parts believable. "Thanks, didi. I'll ask Ravi Uncle too, he's a civil engineer, and my drawing teacher." "Good. Don't take only my word."

qa.q: What did Urmila say she has missed?
qa.a: Urmila said she has missed family dinners.

qa.q: What made Sumit feel something settle?
qa.a: Urmila's honesty about the long studies, the last-minute changes and the missed dinners made her good parts believable, and Sumit trusts honesty more than glamour.

qa.q: What would you advise Sumit to do next before deciding?
qa.a: Hear more voices, such as Ravi Uncle and the drawing teacher, and compare what they say with Urmila's account. 🙂

qa.q: How does Urmila see her role in Sumit's decision?
qa.a: She wants to give an honest picture but not be the only voice; "Don't take only my word" shows it.

grounding: An older cousin in the field gives Sumit an honest picture of a career, and Sumit trusts it and plans to hear other voices.

passage:
Note to myself, after the Eid lunch. Aunty Rukhsana asked again, "Noor got into that top college, so what about Hafsa?" Hafsa's ears went red and her fork stopped. Then she smiled and said, "Noor worked hard. I'm still deciding," and passed the salad. Later on the terrace she was squeezing a cushion. "I wanted to shout," she said. I told her feeling small and angry is human, and that the short answer was a good one. She said next time she will say the same and not compare back. I held her hand, and she laughed a little.
- Nani Zohra

qa.q: Who asked the comparing question at the Eid lunch?
qa.a: Aunty Rukhsana asked it.

qa.q: What was Hafsa feeling as she passed the salad, and what shows it?
qa.a: Hafsa felt small and angry; the red ears, the stopped fork and later "I wanted to shout" and the squeezed cushion show it. 🤍

qa.q: What could Hafsa do at the next gathering?
qa.a: Give the same brief, smiling answer and not compare back, so her path does not become a contest.

qa.q: How might Aunty Rukhsana see her own question?
qa.a: Possibly as ordinary family interest, without noticing it stings; the note does not show her intent.

grounding: At a family gathering Hafsa is compared with a cousin, feels small and angry, and answers briefly with a smile.

passage: At the athletics club the floodlights were still on when Afreen finished her last 200 metres. It was the fourth dawn practice in a row. Her legs shook, but her mind raced: the state trials in March, a national place, and the sick feeling that everyone else was better. "Log," said Coach Jagdish, tapping the notebook. Afreen wrote: "Four sessions, all done. Two clean starts." The coach pointed at the corner. "Chemistry test Thursday?" "Yes." "Then that goes in the log too. Trials are your goal, not your whole life." Afreen exhaled. "I want it so much I'm scared of it." "Good. Keep counting sessions, not medals."

qa.q: How many dawn practices in a row had Afreen done?
qa.a: It was the fourth dawn practice in a row.

qa.q: What does Afreen mean by wanting it so much that Afreen is scared of it?
qa.a: That the wish to reach the trials burns strongly, and so does the fear of not being good enough; the racing mind and the sick feeling show both.

qa.q: Why does Coach Jagdish put the chemistry test in the log too?
qa.a: It keeps a backup plan and the rest of Afreen's life in view, since the trials are a goal and not the whole of life. 😊

qa.q: How might Coach Jagdish see Afreen's fear?
qa.a: As a normal companion to a big goal, best handled by counting sessions instead of medals.

grounding: Afreen has a bold sporting goal and feels fire and dread; daily logging, a backup plan and counting effort are shown.

passage: Rain drummed on the tin roof of the education fair hall as Akash, in a bright college blazer, leaned over the table. "Guaranteed placement, madam. Deposit today by six, or the seat goes to the next student." It was already ten to five. Aparna's palms were damp, and the brochure named no company at all. "I'll pay after I've shown my father," Aparna said. "Then you lose it," said Akash, smiling less. Aparna's phone was at nine percent, but enough to call Papa. "Don't pay anything tonight," Papa said. "We'll ask at your school and visit the college." Aparna slid the brochure into the bag. "Thank you, no."

qa.q: By what time was the deposit due?
qa.a: The deposit was due that day by six.

qa.q: What was Aparna feeling at the table, and how can you tell?
qa.a: Aparna felt nervous and pressured; the damp palms and the need to call Papa show it.

qa.q: What would you advise someone who is pushed to pay money today?
qa.a: Pause, check with parents and the school, visit the place and never pay under pressure. 🤍

qa.q: How might Akash see Aparna's refusal?
qa.a: As a lost quick sale; smiling less after "Then you lose it" suggests annoyance that the pressure did not work.

grounding: An admissions agent promises guaranteed jobs and pushes a same-day deposit; Aparna pauses and verifies with Papa.

passage: Under a dim streetlight after the power cut, the officer raised a torch. "Stop. Where are you going at this hour?" Jaya's heart pounded and the tuition bag felt heavy. The legs wanted to run; Jaya kept them still and took both hands out of the pockets, open and visible. "Good evening, sir. I'm Jaya, coming home from tuition. My house is two lanes ahead." "Bag?" Jaya opened it: notebooks. "May I call my mother? And am I free to go after?" Officer Gautam nodded. "Call. Then I'll walk you to the corner, the lane is dark." Jaya's phone was at five percent, just enough for Mamma's voice, shaky but steady.

qa.q: Where was Jaya coming home from?
qa.a: Jaya was coming home from tuition.

qa.q: What was Jaya feeling when stopped, and what did Jaya do about the urge to run?
qa.a: Jaya felt scared, with a pounding heart, and kept the legs still and hands visible instead of running.

qa.q: What helped keep this stop calm?
qa.a: A polite greeting, giving a name, visible hands, asking if free to go and calling Mamma.

qa.q: How might Officer Gautam see a teenager on a dark lane at night?
qa.a: As someone to check briefly and keep safe; offering to walk Jaya to the corner because the lane is dark shows concern.

grounding: A police officer stops Jaya, whose heart races; Jaya stays calm, polite, gives a name, asks if free to go and calls a parent.

passage:
Dear Damini,
You asked why I crossed the road yesterday when the constable was standing at the corner. Honest answer: since I saw an officer shove the fruit-seller near our market last month, every uniform feels like a warning. I tense up before anyone has done anything. But yesterday I watched that same constable for a while. He walked a lost old woman to the bus stand and held the traffic for her. That doesn't cancel what I saw, and I'll still be careful. But I don't want to treat everyone as a threat when some are doing their job properly. I'm still working it out. Tell me what you think.
Tanvir

qa.q: What did Tanvir see an officer do last month?
qa.a: Tanvir saw an officer shove the fruit-seller near the market.

qa.q: How does Tanvir feel about uniforms, and how is that feeling shifting?
qa.a: Tanvir tenses up at every uniform as if it were a warning, but seeing the constable help a lost old woman makes Tanvir unwilling to treat everyone as a threat.

qa.q: How can Tanvir stay careful without hating everyone?
qa.a: By judging each officer by what they actually do, staying alert and polite, and remembering that one bad moment is not every officer.

qa.q: How might Damini feel on receiving this letter?
qa.a: Probably trusted and thoughtful, since Tanvir shares a hard feeling openly and asks what Damini thinks.

grounding: After seeing bad police behaviour Tanvir sees every uniform as a threat, then starts to stay careful without hating everyone.

passage: Irfan, you asked why I went quiet about that night, so here it is. I'm Abhinav, and we were on the bench outside the bakery after cricket, near eleven, when a jeep stopped. The officer started shouting: "Out this late? You'll spend the night in the lockup!" My knees were shaking. Then a paper was pushed at me. "Sign and you can go." I didn't read it. I said, "Sir, I'd like my father to be here first." My voice cracked, but I said it twice. The officer grumbled, but let me call. Papa came, we went home, and nothing was signed. What stayed with me was this: being scared that night didn't mean I had done anything wrong.

qa.q: Where were the friends sitting when the jeep stopped?
qa.a: They were on the bench outside the bakery after cricket.

qa.q: What was Abhinav feeling that night, and what did Abhinav take from it afterwards?
qa.a: Abhinav was scared, with shaking knees and a cracking voice, and later understood that being scared did not mean being guilty. 🤍

qa.q: What helped Abhinav most in that moment, and why?
qa.a: Staying respectful but asking for Papa before signing; it stopped Abhinav from putting a name to a paper that was never read.

qa.q: How might Papa have seen that night?
qa.a: Probably with worry, since Papa came to the scene; Abhinav does not say more, so the rest is a guess.

grounding: An officer shouts and threatens Abhinav for being out late; Abhinav stays respectful, signs nothing and asks for a parent, learning fear is not guilt.

passage:
Dear Yamini,
You won't believe what happened after the match. I lost my phone in the auto, and I stood at the roadside with no way to call anyone, feeling stupid. A police constable at the crossing noticed and asked what was wrong. She let me use her phone to call Mummy, took my details for a complaint and told me which office to check. Two days later the station called: an auto driver had handed the phone in. I had honestly expected a shrug, and I got kindness. I'll still keep my eyes open, and I know it isn't like this for everyone, but I wanted to say thank you properly, so I went back and did. 🙂
Ramesh

qa.q: What did the constable let Ramesh do?
qa.a: The constable let Ramesh use her phone to call Mummy.

qa.q: What had Ramesh expected, and what was Ramesh feeling afterwards?
qa.a: Ramesh had expected a shrug and instead felt grateful for the kindness; going back to say thank you shows it.

qa.q: Why can Ramesh be grateful and still stay watchful?
qa.a: One helpful officer shows that authority can protect, but it may not be the same for everyone, so trust and scrutiny can sit together. 🙂

qa.q: How might the constable have seen helping Ramesh?
qa.a: Likely as ordinary duty, and Ramesh's thank-you probably meant something to the constable, though the letter does not say.

grounding: An officer helps Ramesh after a lost phone; Ramesh is grateful, sees authority can protect and still stays watchful.

passage: Madhav, sit. You asked why I keep a small notebook, so I'll tell you. I'm Shankar, your uncle. When I was sixteen, after a college fest, some of us from the basti were standing near the gate when a jeep stopped. The boys in the nice car nearby were told, "Go home safely, beta." We were pushed against the wall and called names. I shook with anger, and felt helpless too, because who would listen to me? That night I wrote everything down: the time, the place, what was said. I showed it to my teacher, who took me to a legal aid clinic run by volunteer lawyers. I learned what officers can and cannot do. It didn't undo that night, but I stopped feeling powerless. That's why I still write things down.

qa.q: What did Shankar do that night before anything else?
qa.a: Shankar wrote everything down: the time, the place and what was said.

qa.q: What was Shankar feeling by the gate?
qa.a: Shankar felt angry enough to shake, and helpless, wondering who would listen.

qa.q: What could Madhav do if something like this ever happened?
qa.a: Write down what happened, tell a trusted adult, look for legal aid and learn about rights, as Shankar did.

qa.q: How might the boys in the nice car have experienced the same moment?
qa.a: They were told "Go home safely", so it was probably easy and gentle for them, and they may not have noticed the difference.

grounding: Shankar recalls officers treating rich boys gently and boys from the basti roughly, and channelling anger into records and knowing rights.
